pos: n. (the Hampshire Benedictine nunnery founded c. 986 by Queen Aelfthryth)
etymology: Old English hwer and wiella, the cauldron spring, for the bubbling springs by the Test; recorded as Hwerwyl.
biblical_def: Wherwell Abbey on the river Test in Hampshire was founded about 986 by Aelfthryth, widow of King Edgar and mother of Ethelred the Unready, for Benedictine nuns. Later chroniclers said she built it in penance for her part in the murder of her stepson Edward the Martyr at Corfe in 978, and whether or not the charge was just, the story travelled with the house for five hundred years. Wherwell was well endowed, took the daughters of Hampshire gentry, and was dissolved in 1539, the abbess and her nuns pensioned. Almost nothing of the medieval buildings remains. The dictionary records Wherwell for the founding legend, because an abbey raised to buy off a crime is the medieval system stated in a single building. Scripture allows a guilty conscience no such instrument. David's repentance offers God no masonry, and the gospel's provision is “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8), which cannot be matched with a gift, since “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) forecloses the whole arrangement.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines penance as suffering undergone as an expression of repentance; expiation as atonement for a crime; endowment as the settling of a fund; contrition as deep sorrow for sin; and satisfaction as that which atones.
webster_full: PENANCE, n. The suffering, labor or pain to which a person voluntarily subjects himself, or which is imposed by authority as a punishment for his faults.
EXPIATION, n. The act of atoning for a crime; the means by which atonement for crimes is made.
ENDOW, v.t. To furnish with money or its equivalent, for the support of a church or charitable institution.
CONTRITION, n. The state of being ground or worn; penitence; deep sorrow for sin as an offense against God.
SATISFACTION, n. That which satisfies; amends; atonement for a crime or offense.

Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
Phi 3:9
And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:
Gal 2:16

Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.
corruption_summary: Hampshire Benedictine nunnery founded about 986 by Queen Aelfthryth, said to be in penance for a royal murder; dissolved 1539.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a guilty conscience has only one remedy and it is not a building. Wherwell was raised, if the chroniclers are right, to settle a debt with God, and the gospel answer is “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8) — a gift received, not a payment tendered.

The live temptation is to think the instinct behind the foundation sound and only the amount mistaken. Paul rules out the whole category for himself, “not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law” (Phi 3:9), and states the doctrine twice in the negative, “a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ” (Gal 2:16). An abbey is only a very large and very slow version of what “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) forbids.

pos: n. (the Dorset Benedictine abbey of 987, where Aelfric the homilist was a monk)
etymology: A pre-English river name, the Cerne, probably Celtic carn, a cairn or rocky place; the village is Cerne Abbas, the abbot's Cerne.
biblical_def: Cerne Abbey in Dorset was founded in 987 by Aethelmaer, a West Saxon noble, for Benedictine monks. Its importance to the English church is one man. Aelfric, afterwards abbot of Eynsham and the greatest prose writer in Old English, was a monk at Cerne from about 987 and composed there his two series of Catholic Homilies and his Passiones Sanctorum — sermons in plain English, written expressly so that unlearned people could hear the Scriptures and the faith in their own tongue, at a time when nobody was required to provide them. He also translated large parts of the Pentateuch. The abbey itself lasted until 1539. The dictionary records Cerne for Aelfric's decision, which anticipated by five centuries the thing Tyndale died for. He understood the reason exactly: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.” (Psa 119:130) is a statement about the simple, and an English homily is simply obedience to it. “it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21) licenses the preacher; a tongue the hearer owns is the minimum that licence implies.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a homily as a plain sermon; the vernacular as the native language; to expound as to explain; the simple as the unlearned; and understanding as the faculty of knowing.
webster_full: HOMILY, n. A discourse or sermon read or pronounced to an audience; a plain, familiar discourse on a religious subject.
VERNACULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as one's vernacular tongue.
EXPOUND, v.t. To explain; to lay open the meaning; to clear of obscurity; to interpret.
SIMPLE, a. Artless; unaffected; undesigning; sincere; weak in intellect; not wise or sagacious.
UNDERSTANDING, n. The faculty of the human mind by which it apprehends the real state of things presented to it.
scriptures: The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
corruption_summary: Dorset Benedictine abbey of 987 where Aelfric wrote the Catholic Homilies in plain English and translated much of the Pentateuch.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Aelfric's own reason for writing English. The Psalmist locates the benefit of Scripture precisely where Aelfric aimed it, “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.” (Psa 119:130), and a homily in the hearer's tongue is the shortest route to that result.

The live temptation is to treat the vernacular as a late Protestant innovation. It was not; it was a tenth-century Dorset monk's instinct, and it follows from the mechanism Paul describes, “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17). Hearing requires words a man has, which is why Nehemiah's Levites “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.” (Neh 8:8), and why God is pleased to work by “it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21) rather than by a learned language.

pos: n. (Abbey Dore, the Herefordshire Cistercian house of 1147 whose church was restored for Protestant worship in the 1630s)
etymology: From the river Dore in the Golden Valley, from Welsh dwr, water; the valley name arose from confusing dwr with French d'or.
biblical_def: Abbey Dore in the Golden Valley of Herefordshire was founded in 1147 as a Cistercian house, a daughter of Morimond, and it built in the thirteenth century an ambitious east end with an ambulatory. It was dissolved in 1536 and the nave fell down. What makes Dore unusual is what happened a century later: in 1633 John Scudamore, first Viscount Scudamore, restored the surviving crossing and chancel as a parish church, roofed it, and fitted it with a great carved oak screen by the Herefordshire craftsman John Abel, with communion rails and a holy table. The church is still in use. The dictionary records Dore as the one English Cistercian church refitted for Reformed parish worship, and takes the fittings as the argument. A screen and rails arranged around a table where a congregation hears and communicates is a different building from a choir where monks said offices for the dead. “Let all things be done decently and in order.” (1Co 14:40) authorises the arrangement; “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25) names who it is for.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chancel as the part of a church about the altar; a screen as a partition; a communion as the act of partaking of the Lord's supper; a parish as the precinct of a church; and decently as in a becoming manner.
webster_full: CHANCEL, n. That part of the choir of a church between the altar or communion table and the balustrade that incloses it.
SCREEN, n. Any thing that separates or cuts off inconvenience; a partition; an inclosure.
COMMUNION, n. Fellowship; the act of partaking of the sacrament of the Lord's supper; the celebration of the Lord's supper.
PARISH, n. The precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a secular priest, or the precinct the inhabitants of which belong to the same church.
DECENT, a. Becoming; fit; suitable, in words, behavior, dress and ceremony.
scriptures: Let all things be done decently and in order.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise: be thankful unto him, and bless his name.
corruption_summary: Herefordshire Cistercian abbey of 1147, dissolved 1536, whose chancel was restored as a parish church with a carved screen in 1633.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a building is arranged for whoever is meant to be in it. Dore's 1633 refitting put a congregation where a monastic choir had been, and the apostolic warrant for arranging such things at all is modest and sufficient: “Let all things be done decently and in order.” (1Co 14:40).

The live temptation is to read the restoration as mere antiquarian taste. The fittings say otherwise: a table, rails and a screen are for a people who gather, which is what “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25) requires, and for the practice the first church kept, “in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Act 2:42). The Psalter had already described the posture of the people who come in, “Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise” (Psa 100:4).

pos: n. (the Shropshire abbey of 1135 on the Severn, Savigniac and then Cistercian, noted for its library)
etymology: Old English, probably byldu and waesse, the dwelling by the alluvial land; Domesday Beldewes.
biblical_def: Buildwas Abbey stands on the Severn in Shropshire, founded in 1135 by Roger de Clinton, bishop of Chester, for monks of the order of Savigny, which was absorbed into the Cistercian order in 1147. Its church survives nearly complete to the wall-tops, austere and unornamented in the Cistercian manner. Buildwas is valuable to scholarship for a different reason: an unusual number of its books survive, some forty manuscripts traceable to the house, which has allowed historians to reconstruct the reading of an ordinary English monastery with rare precision — patristic commentary, canon law, medicine, and a good deal of Scripture. It was dissolved in 1536. The dictionary records Buildwas for that library, because the surviving books show what the system had and what it lacked. It had the text in abundance and in Latin; it did not have “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.” (Psa 119:130) working among the simple. “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) was on the shelf, and the shelf was behind a door.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a manuscript as a book written by hand; a commentary as an exposition; patristic is not in Webster, but a father is defined as an ecclesiastical writer of the first centuries; inspiration as the infusion of ideas by a superior power; and profitable as yielding gain.
webster_full: MANUSCRIPT, n. A book or paper written with the hand or pen; a writing of any kind, in opposition to what is printed.
COMMENTARY, n. A comment; exposition; explanation; illustration of difficult and obscure passages in an author.
FATHER, n. The appellation of the first Christian writers who followed the apostles.
INSPIRATION, n. The infusion of ideas into the mind by the Holy Spirit; the conveying into the minds of men, ideas, notices or monitions by extraordinary or supernatural influence.
PROFITABLE, a. Yielding or bringing profit or gain; gainful; lucrative; useful; advantageous.
scriptures: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Eph 6:17
And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God:
corruption_summary: Shropshire abbey of 1135, Savigniac then Cistercian, whose surviving manuscripts reveal the reading of an ordinary English monastery.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that possession of the text is not the same as its circulation. Buildwas owned Scripture and commentary in quantity, and “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) is true of every volume on those shelves. The Psalmist describes what the text does when it reaches people, “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.” (Psa 119:130), and that is the sentence the library could not satisfy.

The live temptation is to credit the monasteries with preserving the Bible and leave the account there. They did preserve it, and the Reformation lived off their copying. But preservation is not the use Scripture prescribes for itself: the Bereans “searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11), and the text is given to a believer as “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph 6:17), which is not a thing to be shelved.

pos: n. (the Somerset Benedictine abbey on the Levels, refounded in the tenth century, dissolved 1538)
etymology: Old English micel and eg, the great island, for the rise above the Somerset Levels.
biblical_def: Muchelney Abbey stood on a low island in the Somerset Levels, a Benedictine house of Saxon origin refounded in the tenth-century monastic revival and given a charter by King Athelstan. It was never large. What survives is remarkable all the same: the abbot's lodging of about 1500, nearly intact, with its fireplaces, its panelled parlour and its stone staircase — a comfortable gentleman's house attached to a monastery. The abbey was dissolved in 1538, and the visitation that preceded it reported the monks keeping poor discipline. The dictionary records Muchelney for the abbot's lodging, because the building is the argument. A rule of poverty and common life had produced, by 1500, a private suite with a good chimney for the superior. The drift was not peculiar to Somerset; it was the normal end of the arrangement, and it is the reason “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works” (Rev 2:5) is the right word for reformation. Christ's complaint at Ephesus is not that the lampstand had moved but that the first works had stopped.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a lodging as a place of rest; an abbot as the superior of an abbey; discipline as instruction and government; declension as a falling off; and reformation as a change from worse to better.
webster_full: LODGING, n. A place of rest for a night, or of residence for a time; temporary habitation; apartments.
ABBOT, n. The superior or governor of an abbey or monastery.
DISCIPLINE, n. Education; instruction; cultivation and improvement; subjection to laws, rules and order.
DECLENSION, n. A falling off; decay; a deviation from rectitude; a sinking into a lower state.
REFORMATION, n. The act of reforming; correction or amendment of life, manners, or of any thing vicious or corrupt.
scriptures: Rev 2:5
Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent.
Rev 3:11
Behold, I come quickly: hold that fast which thou hast, that no man take thy crown.
Gal 6:9
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
corruption_summary: Benedictine abbey on the Somerset Levels with a nearly intact abbot's lodging of c. 1500; dissolved 1538.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the shape of real reformation. Christ does not tell Ephesus to find a new programme but to “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works” (Rev 2:5), and the parallel word to Philadelphia is simply “hold that fast which thou hast” (Rev 3:11). Muchelney's abbot had not abolished the rule; he had quietly stopped keeping it.

The live temptation is to make the comfortable abbot a scandal and stop there, as though stricter observance were the cure. Stricter observance was tried repeatedly across five centuries and produced the next comfortable abbot. The exhortation “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9) assumes the drift and prescribes perseverance, while the standing of every man in the house, abbot and novice, rested on “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9).

pos: n. (the Somerset abbey founded by Alfred the Great about 888 on the marsh island of his refuge)
etymology: Old English aethelinga eg, the island of the princes or nobles; the marshes have since been drained.
biblical_def: Athelney was an island in the Somerset marshes where Alfred of Wessex took refuge in the winter and spring of 878 with a small following, fortified the ground, and raided out from it before the campaign that ended at Edington. About 888 he founded an abbey there in thanksgiving, staffing it at first with foreign monks because, as his own writings complain, there were scarcely any Englishmen left who could read Latin. That complaint is the heart of the matter. Alfred set about translating into English the books he judged most needful for his people — Gregory's Pastoral Care, Boethius, Augustine's Soliloquies, the first fifty Psalms — and said in his preface to the Pastoral Care that they should be put into the tongue we all know. The abbey itself was small, poor, and dissolved in 1539; nothing stands. The dictionary records Athelney for Alfred's preface, which is the earliest royal statement of the principle the Reformation recovered. “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.” (Psa 119:130) is why he did it, and “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17) is why it mattered.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a translation as the act of turning into another language; the vernacular as the native tongue; learning as acquired knowledge; thanksgiving as the rendering of thanks; and needful as necessary.
webster_full: TRANSLATION, n. The act of turning into another language; interpretation; that which is produced by turning into another language.
VERNACULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as our vernacular language.
LEARNING, n. The knowledge of principles or facts received by instruction or study; acquired knowledge or ideas in any branch of science or literature.
THANKSGIVING, n. The act of rendering thanks or expressing gratitude for favors or mercies.
NEEDFUL, a. Necessary, as a supply or expedient; requisite.

So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.

So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Psa 19:7
The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple.
corruption_summary: Abbey founded about 888 by Alfred the Great on his marsh refuge, whose king translated the books he judged most needful into English.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Alfred's, stated in a preface and grounded in a psalm: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.” (Psa 119:130). A king who had seen his clergy unable to read their own service books concluded that the remedy was English, and he was right for the reason Paul gives, “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17).

The live temptation is to treat Alfred as a patron of learning in general and miss what he actually chose to translate: pastoral theology and the Psalms. His model was Nehemiah's, where the Levites “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.” (Neh 8:8), and his confidence was in the instrument itself, “The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul” (Psa 19:7), which converts the soul and does not merely inform it.

pos: n. (the Dorset Benedictine abbey founded c. 1026, remembered for its tithe barn and hilltop chapel)
etymology: Old English, the abbot's burh or fortified place; the name postdates the foundation.
biblical_def: Abbotsbury in Dorset was founded about 1026 by Orc, a Scandinavian retainer of King Cnut, and his wife Tola, who endowed a Benedictine house near the coast behind Chesil Beach. The abbey church is gone, but two of its buildings dominate the village still: an enormous tithe barn, among the largest in England, and St Catherine's Chapel on the hill above, a small heavily buttressed stone chapel built in the fourteenth century as a pilgrimage and beacon chapel. The house was dissolved in 1539. The dictionary records Abbotsbury for the barn and the chapel standing within sight of each other, since between them they state the economy exactly: the tithe came in at the bottom of the hill, and the devotion that justified collecting it was performed at the top. Scripture does not forbid supporting ministry — “he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts” (Mal 2:7) assumes a maintained priesthood. What it refuses is the chapel at the top of the hill functioning as the thing the tithe buys, because “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8) is not for sale and “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.” (Joh 4:24) fixes worship somewhere a hill cannot reach.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a tithe as the tenth part; a barn as a covered building for grain; a chapel as a place of worship subordinate to a church; a beacon as a signal fire; and maintenance as sustenance or support.
webster_full: TITHE, n. The tenth part of the increase annually arising from the profits of land and stock, allotted to the clergy for their support.
BARN, n. A covered building for securing grain, hay, flax, and other productions of the earth.
CHAPEL, n. A house for worship; a building subordinate to a church, or appendant to a larger building.
BEACON, n. A signal erected on an eminence, consisting of a pitch barrel or other combustible matter, to be fired at night.
MAINTENANCE, n. Sustenance; sustentation; support by means of supplies of food, clothing and other conveniences.
scriptures: Mal 2:7
For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts.
Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Joh 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
corruption_summary: Dorset Benedictine abbey of about 1026 whose great tithe barn and hilltop St Catherine's Chapel both survive.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that maintaining a ministry is right and buying a blessing is not. Malachi assumes a supported priesthood whose business is knowledge, “he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts” (Mal 2:7), and the tithe barn at Abbotsbury is not in itself an abuse.

The live temptation is to collapse the two buildings into one judgement. The chapel on the hill was a place to seek favour, and favour is not obtained that way: “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8), with “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) closing the door behind it. Christ, moreover, declines to locate worship topographically at all, “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.” (Joh 4:24), which empties a beacon chapel of the thing it was built to supply.

pos: n. (the Dorset minster, a double monastery from c. 705, from which Leoba went to the German mission)
etymology: Old English Winburne, the meadow stream, from winn and burna; the minster element marks the mother church.
biblical_def: Wimborne Minster in Dorset was founded about 705 as a double monastery, of monks and nuns under an abbess, by Cuthburga, sister of King Ine of Wessex. Its lasting significance is missionary. Leoba, a nun of Wimborne and a kinswoman of Boniface, was summoned by him to Germany about 748 and became abbess of Tauberbischofsheim, one of the leading figures of the Anglo-Saxon mission to the Germans; letters between Wimborne and the mission field survive. The monastery was destroyed by the Danes and refounded as a college of secular canons, dissolved in 1547, after which the great church became and remains the parish church. It keeps a chained library, founded in 1686, and a fourteenth-century astronomical clock. The dictionary records Wimborne for Leoba, because the Anglo-Saxon mission is the medieval church at its best and its warrant is unambiguous. “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19) is a command without a geographical limit, and the women and men who left Wessex for the Rhine were obeying it in the plainest sense.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a minster as a monastery or cathedral church; a missionary as one sent to propagate religion; an abbess as the superior of a nunnery; a mission as a sending forth; and heathen as pagan nations.
webster_full: MINSTER, n. A monastery; an ecclesiastical convent or fraternity; but it is now used for a cathedral church.
MISSIONARY, n. One sent to propagate religion; a person sent by ecclesiastical authority to preach the gospel.
ABBESS, n. A female superior or governess of a nunnery or convent of nuns.
MISSION, n. A sending or delegating; persons sent; commission; the act of sending.
HEATHEN, n. A pagan; a gentile; one who worships idols, or is unacquainted with the true God.
scriptures: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
corruption_summary: Dorset double monastery from about 705, home of Leoba, who went from it to lead the Anglo-Saxon mission in Germany.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the commission itself, which the Anglo-Saxon missions obeyed without any of the later machinery: “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19). Leoba crossed the Channel because Boniface asked and because that sentence had no border in it.

The live temptation is to credit the achievement to the monastic system rather than to the word they carried. The mechanism Paul names is not organisational, “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17), and the charge is simply “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2). The confidence that let a Dorset nun sail for the Rhine is Isaiah's, that the word “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11).

“Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) — the whole of the charge.

pos: n. (the Dorset Benedictine abbey of 980 which became a cell of Tewkesbury in 1102)
etymology: Old English cran and burna, the crane's stream; recorded in Domesday as Creneburne.
biblical_def: Cranborne in east Dorset was founded as a Benedictine abbey about 980 by Haylward Snew, a wealthy thegn, and for a century it was the mother house of a small group of dependencies, among them Tewkesbury. In 1102 the relationship was reversed: Robert FitzHamon raised Tewkesbury to abbey rank and Cranborne was reduced to a priory cell of its own former daughter, the monks moving to Tewkesbury and a handful staying behind. The church remains as the parish church, with Norman work and a fine set of medieval wall paintings. The dictionary records Cranborne for that reversal, which is as neat an illustration as the English church affords of institutions outranking each other by patronage rather than by merit. Scripture arranges the matter differently and says so in the one place it might have endorsed hierarchy. “upon this rock I will build my church” (Mat 16:18) is spoken over a confession and not over an estate, and the apostle's description of the church is of a household, “the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth” (1Ti 3:15), with the truth and not the endowment doing the supporting.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a cell as a religious house subordinate to another; a dependency as that which is subordinate; patronage as the right of presentation; precedence as priority of place; and a pillar as a column or support.
webster_full: CELL, n. A religious house, subordinate to a larger monastery or abbey.
DEPENDENCY, n. A state of hanging down from a supporter; that which is attached to or subordinate to another.
PATRONAGE, n. Support; protection; the right of presentation to a church or ecclesiastical benefice.
PRECEDENCE, n. The act or state of going before; priority; the place of honor.
PILLAR, n. A kind of irregular column, round and insulated, used to support or to adorn a building.
scriptures: And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
Eph 2:20
And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;
corruption_summary: Dorset Benedictine abbey of 980 reduced in 1102 to a cell of Tewkesbury, which had been its own dependency.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the church's solidity is doctrinal and not institutional. Cranborne outranked Tewkesbury and then did not, by a patron's decision. Christ's promise, “upon this rock I will build my church” (Mat 16:18), is given in answer to a confession, and that is where the weight sits.

The live temptation is to look for the true church in a table of precedence. Paul looks for it in a household holding a truth, “the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth” (1Ti 3:15), and refuses any rival basis, “other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1Co 3:11). The only ranking he allows is architectural and already settled: “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone” (Eph 2:20).

pos: n. (the Hampshire Premonstratensian abbey of 1222 whose library catalogue of c. 1400 survives)
etymology: Old English ticce and feld, the kid's field or open land; Domesday Ticefelle.
biblical_def: Titchfield Abbey in Hampshire was founded in 1222 by Peter des Roches, bishop of Winchester, for Premonstratensian canons. It was a moderate house of about a dozen canons for most of its life, but it left one document of first importance: a catalogue of its library made about 1400, listing some two hundred and twenty-four volumes arranged by subject and shelf, with a note of where each stood. It is one of the fullest records of an English medieval library anywhere, and it shows a working collection — Bibles and glosses, sermons, canon law, chronicles, grammar, a little medicine. Titchfield was dissolved in 1537 and converted by Thomas Wriothesley into a mansion, Place House, by driving a gatehouse through the nave. The dictionary records Titchfield for the catalogue, and for what a shelf-list proves: these men could find a text when they wanted one. The question the Reformation pressed was who else could. “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) is a statement about the whole book, and “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.” (Psa 119:130) is a statement about who it is meant to reach.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a catalogue as a list of names or titles; a gloss as a comment or explanation; a shelf as a board for holding things; a grammar as the art of speaking correctly; and a volume as a book.
webster_full: CATALOGUE, n. A list or enumeration of the names of men or things disposed in a certain order.
GLOSS, n. A comment; explanatory remark or note, intended to illustrate the subject.
SHELF, n. A board or platform of boards, elevated above the floor, and fixed on the side of a room.
GRAMMAR, n. The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety or correctness, according to established usage.
VOLUME, n. A book; a primary sense of a roll, as the ancients wrote on long strips of bark or parchment.
scriptures: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.
corruption_summary: Hampshire Premonstratensian abbey of 1222 whose c. 1400 shelf-list of 224 volumes is among the fullest English medieval library catalogues.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Bible was never lost and was never widely available, and both halves must be said. Titchfield's catalogue proves a working collection, and the apostolic claim covers all of it: “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16).

The live temptation is to argue from such catalogues that the late medieval church had no access problem. A shelf-list is a list of what twelve canons could reach. The Psalmist's measure is wider, “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.” (Psa 119:130), the Berean standard assumes a congregation that “searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11), and Paul's charge to “give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13) was given for a people's benefit and not a library's.

“The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.” (Psa 119:130) — a wider measure than a shelf-list.
